newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SICK SAMPRAS BEATS CORRETJA IN FIFTH-SET TIEBREAKER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SICK SAMPRAS BEATS CORRETJA IN FIFTH-SET TIEBREAKER.

text.p: Pete Sampras, sick to his stomach, summoned all his Grand Slam courage on Thursday to beat inspired Spaniard Alex Corretja in a fifth-set tiebreaker that ended a four-hour nine-minute, epic struggle at the U.S. Open.

Sampras vomitted at one juncture and was doubled over in pain after every point of the tiebreak, but saw the longest match of this year's tournament end on a Corretja double fault for 9-7 and a 7-6 5-7 5-7 6-4 7-6 victory that put him into the semifinals.
Top-seeded defending champion Sampras will meet the winner of Thursday's night's quarter-final between fourth seed Goran Ivanisevic of Croatia and unseeded Swede Stefan Edberg.

"This is probably the best match of my career," said the brilliant Corretja, who collapsed to his knees after the final point and then sat slumped in his chair with his head covered in a towel for several minutes.
"Probably the best match and the worst one."
Sampras was helped from the court to rapturous cheers from the Stadium Court crowd.
"A lot of people saw things out there that they will never see in a lifetime," said Paul Annacone, Sampras's coach.
"I'm not sure there are any words to describe what went on out there. It was exhilarating to watch."
Sampras looked in physical trouble for much of the second half of the match.

By the tiebreak, he looked unsteady on his feet. After losing the second point to make it 1-1, Sampras stood beyond the baseline and vomitted, drawing a time warning from the umpire but he battled on.
Corretja, ranked 31st in the world, served an incredible 25 aces in the match and had only been guilty of two double faults until his decisive mistake at the last.
The unseeded Spaniard held match point leading 7-6 in the tiebreaker but Sampras, struggling to suck in air, somehow saved himself with a lunging stab volley.
On the next point, Sampras spun a stunning second serve ace to reach his second match point at 8-7.
Then he watched as Corretja, sent his second serve long against the wretched-looking Sampras and crumbled in disbelief.
"I just wanted to put the ball in and it goes out," said Corretja. "I was just thinking put it in, but I should have gone for my serve and not think of him."
In a trainer's room deep beneath the stadium, Sampras dedicated his thrilling victory to his late coach, Tim Gullikson, who died earlier this year after a long battle with brain cancer.
"This one is for Tim, this one is for Tim," Sampras's girlfriend, Delaina Mulcahy, said the world number one told her.
Sampras also served up 25 aces and needed just about every one of them to keep him in the match as Corretja outplayed him in every other phase of the game.

Playing the match of his life, the Spaniard lashed forehand winners cross court and down the line past the bewildered American and often left Sampras looking like a statue at the net as his angled passing shots whizzed by.
Corretja lashed 90 winners to 74 for Sampras, who began to find the mark only as the end approached, and committed just 30 errors compared to a shocking total of 68 for Sampras.

The Spaniard, who dominated Sampras with his serve in the second two sets, nearly won the first set after breaking Sampras in the opening game. But the American saved two set points serving at 3-5 and then broke in the 10th and forced a tiebreak, which he dominated with his serve.
Sampras won the last 22 points on his serve and in the tiebreak served six times with Corretja managing to put only one back in play.
In the second set, Corretja cracked three ferocious forehand winners on his way to breaking Sampras in the last game.
Corretja again broke Sampras in the last game of the third set for a two sets to one lead as Sampras missed his second easy overhand of the game well beyond the baseline.

Sampras levelled the match in the fourth set with a lone service break in the third game after calling for the trainer during the changeover. A cross court touch volley brought him the break and an ace finished a love service that sealed it 6-4.

The last set stayed on serve throughout, although it was clear Sampras was struggling to stay on his feet. Like two arm weary prize fighters at the end of a brawl, the two offered little resistance on serve until the classic tiebreaker.
Afterwards, tournament doctor Brian Hainline gave Sampras a clean bill of health.
"Pete's fine," said Hainline. "He did require hydration and took two litres of intravenous solution.

"After the first set or two he realised he didn't have the energy he needed. His stomach started getting queasy. He started to get dehyrdrated. At the end, we saw a combination of stomach queasiness and deyhydration.
"There is nothing otherwise medically wrong."
Tom Gullikson, Tim's twin brother and Sampras's Davis Cup coach, saluted Sampras.

"He had reached the boundary and somehow he found a way to extend it and somehow he found a way to will himself to win that match," said Gullikson. "That's all it was, it was just determination and will to win the match.
"At the end it really wasn't even about tennis, even though they happened to be playing tennis."
